name: APT-C-23
iocPatterns: Phishing emails tailored to telecoms and business service sectors
Disguised Android app updates containing spyware
Reused C&C domain infrastructure from earlier VAMP releases
Malicious distribution website impersonating messaging or job application apps
JavaScript downloader scripts used to fetch malware
Hardcoded internal version numbers indicating campaign variants
keyCapabilities: Mobile spyware deployment (GnatSpy, FrozenCell, SpyC23.A, AridSpy)
Backdoor installation & remote command execution (Barb(ie) Downloader, BarbWire Backdoor, Micropsia, VAMP)
Social engineering via fake Facebook profiles and catfishing lures
Downloader‑based delivery using Barb(ie) Downloader and JavaScript downloader myScript.js
Trojanization of legitimate Android applications for distribution
Multistage payload architecture with first‑ and second‑stage components
Persistence through C&C domain reuse and legitimate app updates
Exfiltration of device information via command‑and‑control channel
recommendedActions: Implement advanced phishing detection and filtering to block spear‑phishing emails
Block known malicious domains associated with APT‑C‑23 command-and-control traffic
Deploy mobile device management solutions that detect and isolate mobile spyware (GnatSpy, SpyC23.A)
Conduct regular endpoint monitoring for indicators of trojanized applications masquerading as legitimate apps
Apply timely patches to reduce exploitation surface for remote control payloads
Sandbox and perform static analysis on trojanized Android apps before installation
Monitor network traffic for abnormal downloads from C2 servers and second‑stage payload acquisition
Enable detection capabilities for data exfiltration over command-and-control channels

campaignsText: APT‑C‑23 has maintained a persistent presence in the region, launching coordinated spear‑phishing campaigns since 2015 that target Israeli and Palestinian organizations across multiple industry sectors. The actor employs a modular toolkit, reusing infrastructure from legacy malware families such as VAMP to reduce detection risk while evolving new Android spyware variants for device compromise. Victim profiles include high‑profile government officials, defense contractors, telecom operators, financial institutions, and critical infrastructure entities. Operations exhibit operational tempo that allows for adaptive weaponization across platforms and sustained data exfiltration over command‑and‑control channels.
description: APT‑C‑23, also known as Arid Viper or Bearded Barbie, is a sophisticated Iranian cyber‑espionage group that targets Israeli and other Middle Eastern entities through spear‑phishing campaigns and mobile spyware deployments. The operator focuses on obtaining device identifiers, communications data, and sensitive corporate and government information across sectors such as defense, telecoms, finance, education, and critical infrastructure.
goals: APT‑C‑23’s primary objective is long‑term surveillance of Israeli officials, Palestinian entities, and other Middle Eastern interests. By harvesting device identifiers and intercepting communications, the actor seeks strategic information that aids state‑level intelligence gathering on political, military, and economic targets across government, defense, telecoms, finance, education, healthcare, transportation, media, non‑profit, legal services, critical infrastructure, and manufacturing sectors.
